A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mechanistic forecasting study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A-C support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original probe performance and preference-estimation experiments across seven models and six national elections, including party, persona-attribute and entropy analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds probe comparisons, layer-window experiments, non-political interventions and in-context learning comparisons.

M1.justification: The forecasting procedure remains unchanged: binary probes, the 0.5L-0.9L layer range, 2.5-IQR vector selection, sign-inversion filtering, activation aggregation and entropy gating are retained. The additional interventions validate existing components; the suggested multiclass head remains future work.

E1.justification: The six election datasets, languages and persona attributes remain unchanged. v2 adds a distinct evaluation scenario using 1,280 persona-question pairs with non-political questions, such as choosing ice cream, while measuring party-token responses (Appendix B.5).

E2.justification: v2 retains the probability-based comparator and adds label-shuffled and random-weight probes, hard-label and soft-target regression baselines (Figure 6), no-scaling and matched random-vector controls (Figure 9), and ICL and random forecasting baselines (Figure 10). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce alternative layer-window evaluations, a selectivity-gap metric, matched intervention conditions on identical prompts, and ICL contexts containing one example per party. Figure 6 specifies 4,000 training epochs and a 10% hold-out split for its comparisons. These are additional protocols; the existing forecasting settings and distance metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial validation of probe specificity, sensitivity to layer-window selection, and targeted versus random interventions in non-political contexts (Appendices B.2 and B.5). It also reports inconsistent intervention effects without sign-inversion gating and tests whether supplying party-position information through ICL explains the forecasting advantage (B.6).

E5.justification: v2 adds significance markers to Figures 3 and 5, seeds 0-9 and standard deviations across configurations in Figure 6, permutation tests, one-sided sign-flip tests for layer selectivity, and paired t-tests for interventions. This substantially expands statistical reporting, without establishing increased runs for retained experiments. The tests underlying the new markers in Figures 3 and 5 are not identified.

E6.justification: v2 adds probe-control scores, layer-selectivity results, targeted intervention effects and ICL/random forecasting errors. Figure 6 reports approximately 0.99 macro-F1 for the probe, 0.33 for shuffled labels, 0.24 for random weights and 0.93 for hard-label regression. Soft-target regression is about 0.30, inconsistent with Section 5.1's general regression summary. The retained forecasting plots preserve their estimates.

T1.justification: Figure 7 introduces the selectivity-gap definition, Delta_sel = MacroF1_real - MacroF1_shuffle, for the new layer-window analysis. The forecasting mathematics, assumptions and Equations 1-17 remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and four headline contributions retain their scope. Section 6 adds more specific conclusions that selected vectors directly influence party-token generation and that forecasting gains are not explained by access to external party-position data alone, strengthening the attribution of the retained central claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds mechanism interpretations from the intervention and ICL controls, qualifies the layer range as a tunable default, notes uncertainty about sufficient prompt variation, and discusses multiclass probing as an untested extension. Its impact statement replaces generic language with specific profiling, political micro-targeting and bias concerns. The overall complementary-to-surveys interpretation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 substantially improves documentation through persona-template construction and translation details, native-speaker verification, and multilingual probe prompts showing statement, answer, comment and shuffled party-list inputs (Table 3). It also documents new experimental settings and adds a concrete GitHub link with stated access to templates and harmonized data; v1 only says the code is available on GitHub.

R1.justification: Section 3 newly credits the prompt-template structure to von der Heyde et al. and positions ten prompt variants as exceeding those used in cited comparable studies. The broader related-work argument remains stable. Publication updates, changed author/title metadata and removal of a duplicate reference do not establish new cited works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. v2 makes targeted explanatory expansions, organizes Appendix B into six subsections, rewrites the impact statement, and updates heading capitalization, author order, affiliations and publication information. The expansion largely reflects added scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds the probe-template Table 3 and four substantive displays: Figures 6, 7, 9 and 10. Figures 3 and 5 gain significance annotations, with Figure 3's horizontal scale extended to accommodate them. The original appendix Figures 6-7 and Table 3 are retained as Figures 8 and 11 and Table 4.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation that v1 lacked: probe controls, layer sensitivity, matched interventions and an information-supplying ICL comparator make the mechanistic explanation more assessable. Prompt documentation and a concrete code link also improve reproducibility. The gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the Figure 6 regression-summary discrepancy and underdocumented significance markers. The claim that external data cannot explain the advantage remains stronger than the one-example-per-party ICL comparison establishes.
